sources: Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989, 10.

text: Sovereignty (Sovranty, Lady of Sovereignty, Flaith) is the goddess of the land. In sacred Ireland she was seen as the bride of the king, wedded to him at his inauguration. Her form varies in the tales. She may be the unnamed loathy hag who offers Niall a drink at her sweetwater well and then asks a kiss in return. She may be Eriu, the titular goddess of the island, or fierce and willful Medb, who weds one king after another. Yet the thought beneath each mask is one. The king's duty is to keep the land fertile by righteous rule, to give welcome to all, and to honor the sacred vows and taboos that bind his office. Should he fail, his reign is lost. So it was with Conaire, who broke his vows and died a horrible death. Koch sees the sovereignty goddess as a personification of the land itself or the claim to rule. In the typical tale, the man fated to be king meets a mysterious woman in a real or implied union. She is later revealed to represent the sovereignty of the place he will govern. Sometimes she is ugly until the meeting with the king turns her beautiful. The classic telling survives as Echtra Mac nEchach Muigmedon, the tale of the sons of Eochaid. Modern writers have returned to it often. The same motif runs through folk-tale as the Loathly Lady, best known from Chaucer's Wife of Bath's Tale. Medb, holding a vessel of intoxicating drink as a sign of sovereignty, stands as an archetypal image. The queen of Connacht does not mirror the politics of Iron Age Ireland. She carries literary and mythic meaning instead. Some scholars, such as Patricia Kelly, read her as a negative image of sovereignty in the Tain. Sovereignty also takes equine form in Epona, Rhiannon, and Macha. Georges Dumezil set the horse in the first function of kingship and priesthood. Gerald of Wales described a rite from Donegal in which a king was mated with a mare, which was then slain, cut up, and boiled. The new king bathed in the water. The Vedic rite of the asvamedha is very similar, so the practice seems to belong to the Indo-European heritage. Catherine McKenna links the horse-woman Rhiannon to the prince Pwyll's right to rule and to his growth as a ruler. The sovereignty pattern appears in many women of tradition, from Guenevere to the Cailleach Bherre. Marie Bhreathnach and Marie Herbert read the Morrigan as a sovereignty goddess. In the Battle of Mag Tuired she gives the land to the Tuatha De Danann by coupling with the Dagda at a river ford. Elsewhere she, or a like figure, may watch over the fall of a hero or a king. Greek and Roman accounts of women such as Camma and Cartimandua suggest that linking leading women to goddesses once served a social role as well as a narrative one. Not every scholar accepts the whole pattern. Erica Sessle warns that reading women only through the sovereignty archetype flattens their meaning. Koch concludes that sovereignty is best seen as one important aspect of a figure of many functions, not the whole of that figure.
